title: Erythema nodosum (incl. drug-induced)
summary: Tender red nodules on the shins that bruise as they fade. Causes include streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, pregnancy and drugs such as the combined pill; the work-up looks for the trigger.

glance.think: Painful, warm, ill-defined red nodules on both shins, often with fever or aching joints.
glance.engine: A hypersensitivity reaction in the fat septa (septal panniculitis) to an infection, drug, inflammatory disease or pregnancy.
glance.backbone: Find the trigger (throat swab/ASO, CXR, FBC, CRP, pregnancy test, drug review); rest, elevation, NSAID if suitable; stop a culprit COC.
glance.never_miss: Sarcoidosis with hilar nodes; TB; IBD flare; cellulitis or DVT mistaken for EN.

what: **Erythema nodosum (EN)** is the commonest **septal panniculitis**: a hypersensitivity reaction producing tender red nodules, usually on the shins. It is most common in women aged 20–45.
cause: A delayed hypersensitivity response to many antigens:

list: **streptococcal infection** (the commonest identifiable cause, especially in children)
**sarcoidosis** (Löfgren syndrome — the [skin signs of systemic disease](condition:dermatomyositis) notes)

**drugs** — **oestrogen-containing contraceptives/HRT**, sulfonamides, penicillins/amoxicillin, bromides, minocycline, gold, and newer agents (BRAF inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors, isotretinoin rarely)
Crops of **tender, warm, ill-defined red nodules 1–5 cm** on the **anterior shins**, usually **bilateral**. Less often on the thighs, forearms or trunk.
They evolve through bruise-like colours ("**erythema contusiformis**", photo E02) and resolve in **3–6 weeks without ulceration or scarring**.
Prodrome: fever, malaise, arthralgia (ankles), sometimes before the nodules.
**Unilateral EN is uncommon but described**. A single unilateral lesion makes it essential to exclude the differentials below.

Clinical diagnosis; look for the cause: **FBC, ESR/CRP, U&E/LFT**; **ASO/anti-DNase B** titre ± throat swab; **CXR** (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy — sarcoid/TB/lymphoma) ± serum ACE/calcium; **IGRA**/Mantoux if TB risk; **pregnancy test**; stool culture if diarrhoea; faecal calprotectin if bowel symptoms; urinalysis
**Deep incisional/punch biopsy** (to fat) if atypical — unilateral, ulcerating or persistent >6–8 weeks.

**Case-specific:** she has a **unilateral tender shin lesion** and takes a **COC + tranexamic acid** (both prothrombotic). Apply **Wells/D-dimer and venous Doppler** if there is calf swelling, cord-like tenderness or leg oedema, to exclude **DVT/superficial thrombophlebitis**. The course discussion did not mention this.

head: EN
Cellulitis
Superficial thrombophlebitis / DVT
Erythema induratum (nodular vasculitis)
Other panniculitis
rows: Spreading erythema, fever, portal of entry, raised WCC

differentials: Also: insect-bite reactions, cutaneous PAN (nodules + livedo — the [vasculitis](condition:cutaneous-vasculitis-approach) notes), Sweet syndrome, lipodermatosclerosis.

ol: **Treat the cause.** In this case, **consider stopping the COC**, which is the most likely drug trigger. **Tranexamic acid** is a less established EN trigger but adds thrombotic risk with the COC. **Metformin** is not a recognised cause: **Contraception and cycle control for PCOS:** a progestogen-only method (desogestrel POP, implant, **LNG-IUS 52 mg** — also helps dysmenorrhoea and heavy bleeding), or cyclical progestogen to protect the endometrium. Weight loss and metformin help cycle regularity; **Dysmenorrhoea:** an NSAID such as mefenamic acid or naproxen (both effective for dysmenorrhoea and EN pain); LNG-IUS; Note the **FSRH/BNF caution** about combining tranexamic acid with a COC — prescribe TXA only for heavy menstrual bleeding, at the licensed dose, and not in people at VTE risk
**Symptomatic:** rest, **leg elevation**, compression hosiery (if arterial supply is adequate), cool compresses; **NSAIDs** (ibuprofen/naproxen) for pain if not contraindicated; paracetamol.
**Specialist options:** potassium iodide (rarely used in the UK); colchicine; systemic corticosteroids only after infection (TB, strep) and malignancy are excluded.
**Review in 2–4 weeks.** Persistent or recurrent EN → dermatology/rheumatology; biopsy if atypical.

management: Unilateral swelling with features of DVT (same-day DVT pathway); fever + spreading erythema (cellulitis); BHL on CXR or respiratory symptoms (sarcoid/TB/lymphoma); bowel symptoms (IBD); ulceration (not EN); pregnancy; lesions lasting >6–8 weeks.
Investigation, contraceptive switch (within competence and UKMEC), NSAID analgesia, and referral. Thrombosis assessment through local DVT pathways.
red_flags: EN with cough, breathlessness, weight loss or night sweats: CXR to look for **sarcoidosis, TB or lymphoma**.
Ulcerating or one-sided nodules: not typical EN, so think again (erythema induratum, vasculitis, cellulitis).
pearls: "EN is a **sign, not a diagnosis**" — the job is finding the trigger.
It heals without scarring, but **new crops can appear for several weeks** after the trigger is removed.
In any woman on a COC + TXA with a **tender, red, unilateral leg**, think **clot** before panniculitis.
